Grade 2 · Unit 2-A

Materials and Their Uses

How do we choose and change materials to make useful things?

Everything we use is made of something, and the choice of material matters. You will sort materials by what they are like, pick the best one for a job, take objects apart and rebuild them from the same pieces, and find out which changes from heating and cooling can be undone and which cannot.

In this lesson

  1. Materials have properties we can observe
  2. We choose materials for jobs
  3. Pieces can be taken apart and rebuilt
  4. Heating and cooling can change materials
  5. Try it at home
  6. Check yourself
  7. Play: Rainproof Note

You did this before / what is new. A fair test changes only one thing and keeps everything else the same. You did fair tests in Unit 0 or K2.0; now you use a fair test to choose the best material for a real job.

Concept 1

Materials have properties we can observe

On a northern Michigan beach, you can find Petoskey stones. They are hard, so they do not bend.

A property is something you can see, feel, or test about a thing, like whether it is hard, bendy, or waterproof. Bendy (also called flexible) means it can bend without breaking. Waterproof means water cannot get through.

We can sort materials by things like hard or soft, bendy or stiff, and waterproof or not.

Try it

Sort everyday things into waterproof, bendy and hard bins.

Drag each thing into the bin that matches it.

Waterproof
Bendy
Hard

No mouse? Tap a thing, then tap a bin.

Then pick one thing you did not sort and say which bin it belongs in, and why.

“Put all hard things here.”

Concept 2

We choose materials for jobs

On a rainy Michigan day, you might wear a raincoat to the bus stop.

The best material depends on what we need it to do.

Try it

Guess first: Which material will keep a paper note dry: paper, foil, cloth, or plastic wrap?

What you need:

  • A small spray bottle of water
  • A tray
  • Paper notes about the size of a playing card (about 6 centimeters by 9 centimeters, or 2.5 inches by 3.5 inches)
  • Pieces of paper
  • Foil
  • Cloth
  • Plastic wrap

Do: Put a note on the tray. Cover it with one material. Spray it 3 times from about 30 centimeters (about 1 foot) away. Lift the cover and check the note: dry or wet? Do the same with each material, with a fresh note.

Look for: Which materials left the note dry? Which let water through?

What it shows: The best material depends on the job. For keeping dry, we pick a material that keeps water out.

Safety: Wipe up spills so no one slips.

“Which one keeps the note dry?”

Data

Example results. Your class results may differ.

MaterialTry 1Try 2Try 3Result
PaperWetWetWetWet
FoilDryDryDryDry
ClothDampWetWetWet
Plastic wrapDryDryDryDry

“Foil: dry all 3 tries. Cloth: wet by try 2.”

Real world

A raincoat is soft and bendy, and it keeps rain out. A bike helmet is hard on the outside to protect your head, but most bike helmets have holes that let air in, so rain can get in too. A helmet is not made to keep water out.

“A raincoat keeps water out. A helmet is hard outside.”

Concept 3

Pieces can be taken apart and rebuilt

A Michigan snowman is built from pieces too: three snowballs and a few sticks.

Many objects are made of pieces, and the same pieces can make a new object.

Diagram

Pieces are small parts that join together to make a whole.

“Same pieces. New shape.”

Real world

Five blocks make a house. Take them apart, and the same five blocks can make a car.

“The same blocks can build a car or a house.”

Concept 4

Heating and cooling can change materials

In Michigan, snow melts into puddles on a warm day, and the puddles can freeze again at night.

Melting means a solid becomes a liquid. Freezing means a liquid becomes a solid.

When something is heated or cooled, the change is either physical or chemical.

In a physical change, it is still the same stuff: ice melts into water, and water freezes back into ice. In a chemical change, it becomes something new: a raw egg cooks into a cooked egg, and the cooked egg cannot turn back into raw egg. Ask: can cooling or warming change it back?

Analogy

Bending a paper clip is a physical change. It looks different, but it is still a paper clip. Baking a cake is a chemical change. The batter becomes something new that cannot turn back into batter.

Ask: Is it still the same stuff? If yes, it is a physical change.

“Same stuff, or something new?”

Try it

Guess first: Will the ice turn back into ice after it melts? Will a cooked egg or toast turn back?

What you need:

  • An ice cube in a small cup
  • A freezer or cold spot
  • Butter or crayon wax
  • Pictures of a cooked egg and toast

Do: Put an ice cube in a cup and let it melt (an adult may use warm water). Look at the water. Put the cup in a freezer and check again later. Look at the pictures of an egg before and after cooking, and bread before and after toasting.

Look for: Ice to water to ice again: it goes back. Egg or toast: it does not go back.

Name it: After each change, say physical change or chemical change.

What it shows: Some changes are physical and can be undone. Some are chemical and cannot.

Safety: Adult handles warm things. No tasting.

“Ice becomes water. Water can become ice again.”

Data

Evidence is what we observe that helps answer a question.

ChangePhysical or chemical?BeforeAfterCan it change back?Evidence
Ice cubePhysicalSolid iceWaterYesThe water froze back into ice.
ButterPhysicalSolid butterMelted butterYesIt hardened again when cooled.
EggChemicalRaw eggCooked eggNoIt stayed solid after cooling.
BreadChemicalSoft breadToastNoIt did not become bread again.

“Can it change back? What is your evidence?”

Real world

In Michigan, snow can melt into puddles on a warm afternoon, and the water can freeze into ice again overnight. That is a physical change: the water can turn back into ice.

“Snow melts. Puddles can freeze.”

Hands-on · Design or investigate

Try it at home or in class

Rainproof Note. Problem: a paper note must stay dry. Students sketch, choose two materials, test each with 3 sprays of water, record dry or wet, and choose the best material using evidence. Criteria: the note stays dry, and the cover bends around the note. If two materials both stay dry, the second criterion decides. Constraints: use kit materials and keep the test fair (same number of sprays, same distance).

Try it

What you need

  • Assorted safe objects (wood, plastic, metal, fabric, paper, rubber)
  • Tray
  • Paper notes
  • Spray bottle
  • Foil
  • Cloth
  • Plastic wrap
  • Blocks, beads, or a paper chain
  • Ice cube
  • Small cup
  • Butter or crayon wax
  • Picture cards for a cooked egg and toast
  • Paper
  • Crayons

Safety:

  • Adult handles warm things.
  • No tasting.
  • Wash hands after handling materials, especially food items.
  • No coin cells or magnets are required.
Try it

What you do

1. Sort (10 minutes). Sort objects by hard or soft, bendy or stiff, waterproof or not waterproof.

2. Rainproof Note (20 minutes). Pick two materials. Spray each 3 times from about 30 centimeters (about 1 foot) away. Record dry or wet. Choose the better one.

3. Take apart and rebuild (10 minutes). Use blocks or beads to make something new from the same pieces.

4. Heating and cooling (15 minutes). Watch ice or butter change, then argue: can it change back? What is your evidence?

Words to know

material
what something is made of.
property
something we can observe about it.
waterproof
keeps water out.
bendy (flexible)
bends without breaking.
pieces
small parts that can make a whole.
melt
solid becomes liquid.
freeze
liquid becomes solid.
reversible
can change back.
irreversible
cannot change back.
evidence
what we observe that helps answer.
physical change
a change where the material is still the same stuff.
chemical change
a change where the material becomes something new.
fair test
a test that changes only one thing.
Tutor notes: misconceptions and pacing

Pacing: 5 sessions of 30 minutes.

Common misconceptions to listen for:

  • “We sort materials only by size.” Correct: we sort by properties such as hard, soft, bendy, waterproof.
  • “All changes can be undone.” Correct: physical changes, like melting, can be reversed; chemical changes, like cooking an egg, cannot.
  • “Only water can melt and freeze.” Correct: other materials, like butter, can melt and harden with safe warming and cooling.
  • “Heating only makes things feel warm.” Correct: heating can melt or soften; cooling can harden or freeze.
  • “A material’s job is the same as its property.” Correct: a property describes the material; a job is how we use it.

Limits and cautions:

  • Heating and cooling must stay safe: use ice, room temperature, sunlight, or adult-handled warm water only. Adult handles warm things.
  • If you cannot refreeze live, the provided dataset can still support an evidence-based argument, but live observation is stronger.
  • Blocks, beads, or paper chains work best; avoid glued objects.
  • Food materials are for observing only; no tasting.
  • If a teacher adds a light or magnet extension, use ready-made lamps only and keep magnets away from Chromebooks.
